rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: No direct verse — only the general trade permission (2:275).
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: Istisna has no scriptural text of its own; it enters law through juristic preference, not revelation. Why here: The Qur'an opens the Istisna ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 2:275.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2094

hadith_meta.narrator: Abu Hazim, from Sahl bin Sa'd

rows.detail: The minbar commission, in the Sales chapters. The Prophet commissions the pulpit: 'Order your slave carpenter to make pieces of wood for me so that I may sit on it while addressing the people.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Abu Hazim, from Sahl bin Sa'd. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: an order to manufacture, sent to the owner of a carpenter, with purpose-specification ('so that I may sit on it while addressing the people'); she orders it made of forest tamarisk; it is delivered and installed. Order, spec, make, deliver — the istisna sequence, preserved by Bukhari inside his commercial chapters. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Some men came to Sahl bin Sa`d رضی اللہ عنہ to ask him about the pulpit. He replied, "Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) sent for a woman (Sahl named her) (this message): 'Order your slave carpenter to make pieces of wood (i.e. a pulpit) for me so that I may sit on it while addressing the people.' So, she ordered him to make it from the tamarisk of the forest. He brought it to her and she sent it to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) . Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) ordered it to be placed in the mosque: so, it was put and he sat on it.” It stands in Sales and Trade. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Istisna ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2094, Sales and Trade.

hadith_meta.narrator: Abu Hazim, from his father (Sahl bin Sa'd)
topics_app: The Book of Mosques and Places of Prayer

rows.detail: Sahl's eyewitness account of the commission. Sahl bin Sa'd: 'By Allah, I know of which wood it is made and who made it' — the commissioned manufacture attested by a living witness.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih Muslim was compiled by Imam Muslim (819-875) of Nishapur. It is regarded as one of the two most authentic collections, alongside Sahih al-Bukhari. Narrator: Abu Hazim, from his father (Sahl bin Sa'd). What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: decades later people dispute the pulpit's wood; Sahl settles it as the last eyewitness — the Prophet 'sent a person to a woman asking her to allow her slave, a carpenter, to work on woods (to prepare a pulpit) so that I should talk to the people'. Maker, commissioner and material all identifiable — the traceability istisna doctrine later demands of specifications. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Some people came to Sahl b. Sa'd and began to differ about the wood of which the (Prophet's pulpit was made. He (Sahl b. Sa'd) said: By Allah, I know of which wood it is made and who made it, and the day when I saw the Messenger of Allah ( ‌صلی ‌اللہ ‌علیہ ‌وسلم ‌ ) seated himself on it on the first day. I said to him: O Abu Abbas (kunyah of Sabl b. [...]” It stands in The Book of Mosques and Places of Prayer. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Istisna ladder; shown at 610 (dated 610-622, medium confidence; shown at the earliest year). Source: Sahih Muslim 1216.

rows.name: Sahih Muslim 5477

topics_app: The Book of Clothes and Adornment

rows.detail: The signet ring made to order, with an exclusivity clause. A ring 'made for himself' of silver, engraved 'Muhammad, Messenger of Allah' — with the order that no one engrave its like.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih Muslim was compiled by Imam Muslim (819-875) of Nishapur. It is regarded as one of the two most authentic collections, alongside Sahih al-Bukhari. Narrator: Ibn Umar. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: a gold ring made and discarded, then a silver one made to order with a specified engraving, plus a uniqueness command — 'No one should engrave anything like the engraving of this signet ring of mine.' A made-to-specification object with an exclusivity condition attached: the classical jurists' second stock example (with the minbar) for manufacture-on-order. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Allah's Apostle ( ‌صلی ‌اللہ ‌علیہ ‌وسلم ‌) had made for himself a gold ring; then he discarded it, and then made for himself a silver ring, and had these words engraved upon it (Muhammad, Messenger of Allah ﷺ), and said: No one should engrave anything like the engraving of this signet ring of mine. And when he wore it, he kept its stone towards the inside of his palm, and it was this which fell down (from the hands) of Mu'ayqib into the well of Aris.” It stands in The Book of Clothes and Adornment. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Istisna ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Muslim 5477.

rows.name: al-Kasani
rows.detail: Al-Kasani's decisive text: istisna fails strict analogy but stands by istihsan — 'people have consensus of practice on it.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kasani (d. 587 AH / 1191 CE) was a jurist of the Hanafi school and author of Bada'i al-Sana'i, a work that draws heavily on al-Sarakhsi's al-Mabsut. What: Bada'i 5/2 is the passage the whole contract hangs on: by qiyas istisna should be void (sale of the non-existent), but juristic preference validates it because unbroken public practice amounts to consensus. A Hanafi contract; other schools folded it into salam; later Hanafis made it binding on both sides. In the work itself (near vol. and page 5:2; our literal translation from the Arabic): “For knowing the issues of this book there is need of an explanation of the form of istisna' and its meaning, and of an explanation of its permissibility, and of an explanation of its ruling, and of an explanation of its character.” It also states: “Some of them [the mashayikh] said: it is a mutual promise and is not a sale; and some of them said: it is a sale, but the buyer has an option in it; and that is the correct [view].” It also states: “Some of them said: it is a contract on a sold thing in liability [dhimma]; and some of them said: it is a contract on a sold thing in liability in which the work is stipulated.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Istisna ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1191 (standard references). Source: Bada'i al-Sana'i, 5/2.

rows.name: OIC Fiqh Academy
rows.detail: OIC Resolution 65 (3/7), 7th session (Jeddah, May 1992): istisna is binding when subject, specs and price are fixed.
rows.detail_long: Who: The International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC issues numbered resolutions at its sessions; AAOIFI's standards cite them. What: The resolution turns istisna from a revocable Hanafi allowance into a binding modern contract — the basis of project and housing finance. The official IIFA records place Resolution 65 (3/7) in the 7th session, Jeddah, 9-14 May 1992. Confirmed on the Academy's official site (iifa-aifi.org). In the source's own words (International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC) - Resolution No. 65 (3/7) Istisna' (Manufacturing) Contract): “First: Istisna' contract, which has been mentioned with regard to work and goods on credit, is binding on both parties if it meets the basic requirements and conditions.” “Second: The Istisna' contract must fulfill the following requirements: A clear statement of the nature, type, amount and required specifications of the product to be manufactured. A specification of the” “Third: In the Istisna' contract, it is permissible to defer payment in full or in installments according to predetermined installments and specific deadlines.” “Fourth: In the Istisna' contract, it is permissible to include a penalty clause if both contracting parties agree, unless subject to force majeure.” Not confirmed by the source read: The page does not print 'price' among the two listed requirements. The second requirement is cut off on the page after 'A specification of the' (the missing word was not seen). Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Istisna ladder; shown at 1992 (7th session, Jeddah, 7-12 Dhu al-Qi'dah 1412 / 9-14 May 1992 (official IIFA records)). Source: OIC Resolution 65 (3/7), 7th session (Jeddah, May 1992).

rows.timeline_year_basis: Adopted as rules 19-23 May 2001 (meeting 6); readopted as a Standard at meeting 8, 11-16 May 2002
rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 11 (Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a) — project and housing finance.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS11 codifies istisna and parallel istisna for construction and manufacturing finance. Rules adopted 23 May 2001, reformatted as Standard 16 May 2002. Clauses read in the standard's text: 3/1/1 istisna'a is valid only for raw materials transformed by a manufacturing or construction process involving labour; 4/1/1 the parties may agree to amend specifications and conditions after conclusion; 5/1 a technically experienced consulting firm may be appointed to verify conformity to specification; 6/1 the manufacturer is discharged on delivery to the purchaser, his appointee, or on the purchaser's full control; 7/1 the Institution may buy on clear, unambiguous specification and pay cash to give the manufacturer liquidity. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Istisna ladder; shown at 2002 (adopted as rules 19-23 May 2001 (meeting 6); readopted as a Standard at meeting 8, 11-16 May 2002). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 11 (Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a).

rows.name: Industry practice
rows.detail: Istisna today is the project and construction contract: infrastructure, home-building and manufacturing finance, usually as istisna + parallel istisna.
rows.detail_long: Who: This rung is a snapshot of how the contract is used in the market today. It is a description of practice, not a ruling. What: Modern usage: the bank contracts istisna with the customer and a parallel istisna with the builder/manufacturer — the structure SS11 clause 7/1 anticipates. Why here: 'Where it stands today' rung of the Istisna ladder; shown at 2024 (current period marker (2024)). Source: Industry practice (descriptive).
